newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Uncertainty clouds outlook for weary Swiss franc.
newsitem.headline: Uncertainty clouds outlook for weary Swiss franc.

text.p: Poor fundamentals and the market's love affair with the dollar have combined to hammer the Swiss franc. Analysts see a bottoming out soon, but varied economic senarios make for a cloudy long-term outlook.

The week began with analysts predicting a franc consolidation. But the consolidation seems to have come and gone unnoticed and the market talks now of a dollar level around 1.50 francs in the not too distant future.
The dollar topped 1.43 Swiss francs on Wednesday, rising to levels not seen since late April 1994.
The U.S. currency traded as high as 1.4360 francs in the morning, up from an opening level of 1.4215/4225 in Zurich.

The dollar gained further against the franc and against most other currencies following Tuesday's comments from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan, who said in his senate testimony that U.S. growth was still strong.

Speculation about U.S. credit tightening to cool a heated economy, coupled with the poor prospects for Swiss growth, could lead to further interest rate gap widening between the two currencies, to the detriment of the franc, analysts said.

Union Bank of Switzerland currency analyst Hans Scherer sees the franc moving to a 1.4500/1.5000 range to the dollar within the next six months, then back down, levelling off at 1.4500 by the end of the year.
He forecast a mark/Swiss move to around 88.00 centimes before easing back to 86.00/87.00 by year's end.

Resumption of economic growth should lead to a firmer franc. But the chances for a rebound sufficient to lead to more restrictive monetary policy and a higher franc seem less likely now than they did last year.
The Swiss economic institute KOF this week cut its 1997 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) forecast to zero growth from a previous estimate of 0.9 percent growth
"The KOF revision was a bit sobering," Scherer said.

In view of the poor outlook the Swiss National Bank (SNB) is likely to stick to its relatively neutral policy stance after having dropped the discount rate from 3.5 percent in the summer of 1995 to the current 1.0 percent level.
In addition, SNB board member Bruno Gehrig said on Monday that the central bank would continue its current monetary policy of controlled expansion.

Other analysts, who judge the prevailing outlook to be a bit too pessimistic, say the franc has gone the full cycle, is now undervalued, and should slip back to levels seen in December 1996 by the end of this year.

Measuring the franc against other currencies on the basis of Purchasing Power Parity (PPP), the dollar should be at a level of about 1.33 francs and the mark at roughly 83.91, said Swiss Bank Corp economist Janwillem Acket.
"From a fundamental point of view there is no reason to think that we are in for a Swiss franc free-fall," Acket said.
Signs of better economic activity should result in a shift by the central bank to a neutral from an expansionary policy and this should give the franc a boost.
"This will happen, at the earliest, in the second half of this year," Acket said.
He said SBC is forecasting a dollar/Swiss rate falling back to 1.3800 within the next three months, 1.3500 in six months time and 1.3300 by the end of the year.

Looking at the franc against the other currencies in Europe, Acket pointed out that chances of foreign exchange turbulence leading up to the introduction of the EU's single currency is still an unknown factor which could lead to unpredictable swings of the franc.

"This could go both ways. But given the current fundamentals there is a downside risk for the others (currencies) and we are an alternative," he said, adding, "In 12 months time our economy has a chance of being in fairly good shape. -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
